segments.literal: then you-will-be-cleared from-my-oath when you-come to my-clan and-if not they-will-give to-you and-you-will-be clean from-my-oath

tokens.note: 3rd person plural: 'they' are the kin named in 24:41.7; the object is not written.
waw with the perfect: a future in sense, 'and you shall be'.

phrases.english: Then you will be clear of my oath
phrases.literal: then you-will-be-cleared from-my-oath; the nifal of נָקָה, 'to be cleared' of an obligation

phrases.english: when you come to my kin
phrases.literal: when you-come to my-clan; כִּי with the imperfect makes the going the condition

phrases.literal: and-if not they-will-give to-you; the Hebrew names no object for 'give'

phrases.english: you will be clear of my oath

grammar: תִּנָּקֶה is nifal yiqtol of נָקָה: 'be free from an obligation' (Niph 4), with מֵאָלָתִי the thing one is freed from.
The accents divide the verse at תָּבוֹא (tipḥa) and at מִשְׁפַּחְתִּי (etnaḥta): the going to the clan, then the conditional clause from וְאִם־לֹא.
The conditional clause וְאִם־לֹא יִתְּנוּ לָךְ names no object for the giving; the English adds none.
וְהָיִיתָ נָקִי is a waw-qatal with future force, repeating the verdict of the first clause.
segments.note: The word is אָלָה, 'oath' with its curse (BDB senses 1 and 3). Ibn Ezra, the one normative commentator, notes that the verse does not say שבועה and gives the servant's fear of his master as the reason (commentary below); the English 'oath' is the lexicon's first sense.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra notes that the verse says מֵאָלָתִי and not מִשְׁבוּעָתִי ('from my swearing'), and gives the reason: the servant fears his master and his אָלָה (oath with its curse).

context: In the ancient Near East an oath could carry a curse on whoever broke it. Hebrew אָלָה covers both the oath and the curse, and the lexicon gives both; the English 'oath' is the undertaking that binds the servant to his master.

segments.english: I came today to the spring and I said, 'LORD, God of my master Abraham, if you are now making my journey successful, the one on which I am going—
segments.literal: and-I-came the-day to the-spring and-I-said the-LORD God-of my-master Abraham if there-is-you now making-successful my-journey which I going upon-it

tokens.note: wayyiqtol: the narrative 'and I came'.
wayyiqtol, first person singular.
the name with the title אֱלֹהֵי: II.1 (used with אלהים).
יֶשְׁךָ: יֵשׁ with a suffix; with the participle that follows it makes a periphrasis, 'you make ... succeed'.

phrases.english: I came today to the spring
and I said, 'LORD, God of my master Abraham,
phrases.literal: and-I-said the-LORD God-of my-master Abraham; the prayer opens with the name and its title, an address

phrases.english: if you are now making my journey successful,
the one on which I am going—
phrases.literal: which I going upon-it; 'upon it' refers back to the feminine דֶּרֶךְ

grammar: וָאָבֹא and וָאֹמַר are wayyiqtol forms: the narrative of the servant's report, 'I came ... and I said'. The prayer that begins here runs to the end of 24:44.
יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי אֲדֹנִי אַבְרָהָם is an address: the name, then the title in a construct chain; English gives it no article.

אִם־יֶשְׁךָ־נָּא מַצְלִיחַ: יֵשׁ with a pronoun suffix (יֶשְׁךָ, 'you are') and a participle makes a present condition, 'if you are now making successful'. The sentence breaks off, and the prayer goes on in 24:43.
עָלֶיהָ ('upon it') refers back to the feminine דֶּרֶךְ, so the relative clause closes on the way.

commentary.summary: Rashi glosses the word for today as 'I went out today and I came today', and cites a midrash that the earth was folded up for him. This is a homily on the journey, not a reading of the words.

segments.english: Here I stand by the spring of the water, and it shall come to pass that the young woman who comes out to draw, and I will say to her, "Please give me a little water from your jar to drink,"
segments.literal: here I standing upon the-spring-of the-water and-it-shall-be the-young-woman the-going-out to-draw and-I-will-say to-her give-me-to-drink please a-little water from-your-jar

tokens.note: participle with הִנֵּה: the present scene, 'here I stand'.

tokens.gloss: and it shall come to pass that
tokens.note: waw with the perfect introducing the sign: 'and it shall come to pass'.
waw with the perfect: future in sense.

phrases.english: Here I stand by the spring of the water,
phrases.literal: here I standing upon the-spring-of the-water

phrases.english: and it shall come to pass that the young woman who comes out to draw,
and I will say to her,
"Please give me a little water from your jar to drink,"

grammar: הִנֵּה with the participle נִצָּב gives the present scene: 'here I stand'.
וְהָיָה with a following clause introduces the sign: 'and it shall come to pass that'; the waw-qatal is future in sense, and the verb is masculine before the feminine הָעַלְמָה.
The sentence opens with the young woman and has no main verb of its own; it is completed by הִוא הָאִשָּׁה in 24:44. The English leaves it open as the Hebrew does.
The tipḥa on נִצָּב and the etnaḥta on הַמָּיִם divide the scene from the sign; the request is the clause from הַשְׁקִינִי־נָא.
The imperative הַשְׁקִינִי is the Hiphil of שָׁקָה, 'give drink to', with 'a little water' as its object: 'give me a little water to drink'.
context: A jar carried on the shoulder was the ordinary water vessel of the period; the verse names no other vessel.

segments.english: and she will say to me, "You also drink, and I will draw for your camels also"—she is the woman whom the LORD has appointed for my master's son.'
segments.literal: and-she-will-say to-me also you drink and-also for-your-camels I-will-draw she the-woman which has-appointed the-LORD for-son-of my-master

tokens.note: waw with the perfect: future in sense.
Qal imperative, masculine singular, of שָׁתָה: 'drink'.
Hiph of יָכַח; Rashi reads 'chose and made known' (commentary).

phrases.english: and she will say to me,
"You also drink,
phrases.literal: also you drink; the girl's words

phrases.english: and I will draw for your camels also"
—she is the woman
phrases.literal: she the-woman; a nominal clause, the English supplies 'is'

phrases.english: whom the LORD has appointed for my master's son.'

grammar: וְאָמְרָה is a waw-qatal, future in sense: 'and she will say', the sign he set.
שְׁתֵה is the Qal imperative of שָׁתָה, 'drink', addressed to the servant.
הִוא הָאִשָּׁה is a verbless clause: the pronoun, then the article-noun. English supplies the copula: 'she is the woman'.
The etnaḥta on אֶשְׁאָב divides the sign from the identification; the zaqef qaton on הָאִשָּׁה sets off the relative clause.
גַּם occurs twice (גַּם אַתָּה, וְגַם לִגְמַלֶּיךָ); the English keeps 'also' in both places.

commentary.summary: Rashi reads גַּם in גַּם אַתָּה as including the men who were with the servant. The English keeps 'also' as the servant's own request and records Rashi's reading here.
Rashi glosses הוֹכִיחַ as בֵּרֵר וְהוֹדִיעַ, 'chose and made known'. The English 'has appointed' takes this sense of choosing (Hiph 2).

Sforno cites the tradition of a heavenly voice declaring 'בַּת פְּלוֹנִי לִפְלוֹנִי' (the daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so) and reads הִיא הָאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר הוֹכִיחַ as that declaration. This is a homily on the verse, not a reading of its words.

context: Camels as pack and riding animals in the patriarchal period are disputed: some hold that domestic camels came into common use in the Near East only after the patriarchs' time, others that earlier use is attested. The text is translated as it stands, and the question is left open.

segments.english: Before I had finished speaking to my heart, look, Rebekah was coming out, with her jar on her shoulder; and she went down to the spring and drew, and I said to her, 'Give me a drink, please.'
segments.literal: I before I-finish to-speak to my-heart and-look Rebekah coming-out and-her-jar upon her-shoulder and-she-went-down to-the-spring and-she-drew and-I-said to-her give-me-to-drink please

tokens.note: yiqtol with טֶרֶם: 'before I finish'; the English takes the narrative past.
The entry's headword gloss is 'shoulder'; of its printed senses, 1 'neck' and 2 'back', neither is the shoulder, so none is given.
wayyiqtol.

phrases.english: Before I had finished speaking to my heart,
phrases.literal: I before I-finish to-speak to my-heart

phrases.english: look, Rebekah was coming out,
with her jar on her shoulder;
and she went down to the spring and drew,
and I said to her, 'Give me a drink, please.'

grammar: טֶרֶם with the imperfect אֲכַלֶּה means 'before I finish'; Rashi's reading of this present-tense form is in the commentary.
The sentence opens with the fronted pronoun אֲנִי; the revia on לִבִּי closes the opening clause, and וְהִנֵּה begins the scene.

וְהִנֵּה with the participle יֹצֵאת gives the scene: 'look, Rebekah was coming out'; the participle needs no finite verb in Hebrew, and English supplies 'was'. וְכַדָּהּ עַל־שִׁכְמָהּ is a circumstantial clause: 'with her jar on her shoulder'.
The etnaḥta on וַתִּשְׁאָב ends the first half of the verse.
The Hebrew names no object for שָׁאַב ('draw'); the English keeps it so.

commentary.summary: Rashi says that אֲכַלֶּה is to be read as the present, 'before I am finishing': every such present-tense expression may be worded in the past (כִּי אָמַר אִיּוֹב) or in the future (כָּכָה יַעֲשֶׂה אִיּוֹב), and the meaning of both is the ongoing present ('Job used to say ... and used to do so'). The English takes the narrative past, 'had finished', and records Rashi's reading.
Ramban explains how the servant knew her name: either he heard it while at her house, or she told him her name at first, though the text does not record it.
Sforno calls the sequence of events a sign (הוֹרָאָה) that the matter is right from God (נָכוֹן הַדָּבָר מֵעִם הָאֱלֹהִים).

context: A jar (כַּד) carried on the shoulder was the ordinary water vessel of the period; the verse names no other vessel.

segments.english: She hastened and took down her jar from upon her, and said, 'Drink, and I will water your camels also.' And I drank, and she watered the camels also.
segments.literal: and-she-hastened and-she-took-down her-jar from-upon-her and-she-said drink and-also your-camels I-will-water and-I-drank and-also the-camels she-watered

tokens.note: wayyiqtol.
wayyiqtol of יָרַד with the hifil: 'took down' the jar.
Qal imperative, masculine singular, of שָׁתָה: 'drink'.
wayyiqtol, 1st person singular, of שָׁתָה (short form וָאֵשְׁתְּ): Qal 'drink'.

phrases.english: She hastened and took down
her jar from upon her,
and said, 'Drink,
and I will water your camels also.'
And I drank, and she watered the camels also.

grammar: Three wayyiqtol forms in a row (וַתְּמַהֵר, וַתּוֹרֶד, וַתֹּאמֶר) narrate the girl's haste.
שְׁתֵה is the Qal imperative of שָׁתָה, 'drink'; וָאֵשְׁתְּ is its wayyiqtol in the first person (short form), 'and I drank'.

שָׁקָה (Hiphil, 'give drink to, water') is the servant's verb in 24:43 and 24:45 (הַשְׁקִינִי); the girl uses it for the camels: אַשְׁקֶה (yiqtol, 'I will water') and הִשְׁקָתָה (qatal, 'she watered').
Both camel clauses begin with גַּם and put the camels first; English places 'also' at the end.
The revia on וַתְּמַהֵר and the zaqef gadol on וָאֵשְׁתְּ divide the verse; the silluq on הִשְׁקָתָה closes it.

segments.english: I asked her and I said, 'Whose daughter are you?' And she said, 'Daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.' And I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her hands.
segments.literal: and-I-asked her and-I-said daughter-of whose you and-she-said daughter-of Bethuel son-of Nahor which bore to-him Milcah and-I-put the-ring upon her-nose and-the-bracelets upon her-hands

tokens.note: wayyiqtol: 'inquire of' the woman.
Abraham's brother, the second sense of the name in the lexicon.
wayyiqtol: 'put upon'.

phrases.english: I asked her and I said,
'Whose daughter are you?'
phrases.literal: daughter-of whose you; a nominal question

phrases.english: And she said,
'Daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.'
phrases.literal: daughter-of Bethuel son-of Nahor who bore to-him Milcah

phrases.english: And I put the ring on her nose
and the bracelets on her hands.

grammar: בַּת־מִי אַתְּ is a nominal question. English needs 'are'; the Hebrew has no verb.
The chain בַּת־בְּתוּאֵל בֶּן־נָחוֹר keeps its construct form: 'daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor'.
The relative clause אֲשֶׁר יָלְדָה־לּוֹ מִלְכָּה follows the names in Hebrew as in English: 'whom Milcah bore to him', לוֹ being Nahor.
The verb וָאָשִׂם ('I put') follows the question and answer in Hebrew order; the English keeps that order.

commentary.summary: Rashi says the order is changed: the servant first gave the ring and afterwards asked, but he tells it in the other order so that they could not catch him in his words and say, 'How did you give to her when you did not yet know who she was?' The English keeps the Hebrew order, the order the words give; the explanation of what happened is recorded here only.

context: Rings and bracelets were worn by women in the ancient Near East; the verse does not say what metal they were made of.

grammar: וָאֶקֹּד and וָאֶשְׁתַּחֲוֶה are wayyiqtol narrative forms; the second is hishtafel, reflexive, hence 'prostrated myself'.
לָקַחַת with its object בַּת־אֲחִי אֲדֹנִי is the purpose of the leading; לִבְנוֹ closes the phrase: 'for his son'.
The etnaḥta on לַיהֹוָה ends the first half of the verse; the pashta on יְהֹוָה sets off the title; the silluq on לִבְנוֹ closes the verse.
apparatus: 24:48.3 vowels: WLC reads לַיהוָה; base לַיהֹוָה. The name is the same in both; the English is unchanged.
